learning_objective: 🎯 Discover the 'why' behind motion! Master Newton's three legendary laws, understand the concept of inertia, and learn how friction shapes our physical world.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion with the same speed and in the same direction unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force. Mass is the measure of inertia.

The real definition: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force ($F = dp/dt$). For a constant mass, this simplifies to the famous formula: $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$.
To every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction. Crucial detail: Action and reaction forces act on DIFFERENT bodies, which is why they do not cancel each other out!
Momentum ($p = mv$) is the 'quantity of motion'. Impulse is a huge force acting for a very short time (like a bat hitting a cricket ball). Impulse equals the change in momentum.

The invisible force resisting motion. 'Static friction' is a self-adjusting force that stops things from sliding. Once an object starts moving, it becomes 'Kinetic friction', which is always slightly weaker than maximum static friction.

fun_activity.title: 🪙 The Coin & Card Trick
fun_activity.instructions: Place a smooth playing card over the mouth of a glass. Place a heavy coin in the center of the card. Flick the card hard horizontally with your finger. The card flies away, but the coin drops straight into the glass due to its 'Inertia of Rest'!

exam_tips: 📌 Free Body Diagrams (FBD) are essential! Always draw the object isolated with arrows for gravity ($mg$), Normal force ($N$), Applied Force, and Friction.
📌 Law of Conservation of Momentum is frequently asked. If no external force acts on a system, its total momentum remains constant ($p_i = p_f$).
📌 Banking of roads derivation: $v_{max} = \sqrt{rg \tan\theta}$ is a highly probable 3 or 5-mark question.
quick_recap: ⭐ Force is a vector; it requires both magnitude and direction to be fully described.
⭐ A passenger falling backward when a bus starts moving is a classic example of Inertia of Rest.
⭐ The coefficient of static friction ($\mu_s$) depends only on the nature of the two surfaces in contact, not on the area of contact.
